card.tagline: A Turkish kochari circle dance echoing globally across Turkish, Assyrian, and Greek adaptations.
card.profile: Elazığ dik halay, also known as Karaçor or Karachor, is a Turkish kochari folk dance performed in a circle. Its traditional melodies are linked to folk songs known as Shoror. Over time, the tune has crossed linguistic and national boundaries, inspiring modern adaptations in Turkey, Russia, and Greece. These versions range from Barış Manço's Turkish interpretations to Assyrian recordings by Loudmila Khoshaba and Greek pop releases.
card.insight: A single folk melody from Elazığ travels across borders, surfacing as Barış Manço's Turkish rock, Loudmila Khoshaba's Assyrian pop, and Katy Garbi's Greek dance track.
card.profile_long:
Elazığ dik halay, which is also identified in traditions as Karaçor or Karachor, stands as a notable example of a Turkish kochari folk dance structured around a circle dance formation. Within the documented cultural landscape, this dance is intrinsically tied to related folk songs known as Shoror. While technical details regarding its specific physical execution, footwork, costume, and musical instrumentation remain unrecorded in the primary literature, its cultural footprint is exceptionally vast through its musical diaspora and contemporary popular adaptations.

The melodic and structural lineage of Elazığ dik halay has transcended regional and national boundaries, undergoing fascinating transmutations across multiple linguistic traditions. In Turkey, modern popular versions of the underlying song feature Turkish lyrics and are widely recognized under the title 'İşte Hendek İşte Deve'. Among the prominent interpreters of this version is the celebrated Turkish artist Barış Manço, who brought the folk melody into the realm of modern popular music.

The journey of the melody extends far beyond Turkish borders into international music markets. In Russia, the tune was adapted with Assyrian lyrics and released under the title 'Kochari'. This rendition is notably performed by Loudmila Khoshaba, appearing as a track on her 2008 album titled 'Nazdarta'. This cross-cultural migration illustrates how folk motifs from Elazığ found resonance within Assyrian communities abroad, bridging regional heritage with contemporary eastern European and Russian diaspora production standards.

Further south and west, the melody also established a permanent foothold in the Greek music scene. In Greece, the tune was adapted with Greek lyrics under the title 'Agkires', which translates to 'Anchors'. This Greek iteration was famously recorded by pop artist Katy Garbi and released on her 1999 album 'Doro Theou'. The creation of this version involved specific artistic contributions from the Greek musical establishment: the album track was composed in Greece by Savvas Angin, while the Greek lyrics were penned by Eleni Gianatsoulia. 

Despite the extensive documentation of these modern pop, rock, and international variants, the traditional practice of Elazığ dik halay itself suffers from significant documentation gaps. The sources provide no descriptions concerning the exact tempo, musical meter, rhythm patterns, costume design, or the specific movement vocabulary required by dancers. Consequently, while the global life of its music is thoroughly mapped through recorded albums and cross-cultural covers, the foundational folk dance steps remain preserved primarily within living community memory rather than academic or technical texts.

claims.text: Elazığ dik halay is a Turkish kochari folk dance.
It is a form of circle dance.
There are related folk songs known as Shoror.
Modern popular versions with Turkish lyrics are known as İşte Hendek İşte Deve.
One of the Turkish versions is sung by Barış Manço.
Assyrian lyric versions are known as Kochari in Russia and sung by Loudmila Khoshaba.
Kochari is featured on Loudmila Khoshaba's 2008 album Nazdarta.
Greek lyric versions are known as Agkires in Greece and sung by Katy Garbi.
Agkires appears on Katy Garbi's 1999 album Doro Theou.
The Greek song was composed by Savvas Angin.
The Greek lyrics were written by Eleni Gianatsoulia.
